scope: Limited file-level owner comparisons and two newly authored draft historical contexts. Absence in a checked file is not a repo-global missing-feature certification.

comparisons.candidateDifference: A potentially additive sourced day-specific explanation about the baptismal white garments and station at St Pancras.

comparisons.candidateDifference: The Mass commentary's prayer-in-Christ's-name reading may enrich that Sunday, but no new Rogation custom or processional trigger is needed.

comparisons.candidateDifference: Historical catechetical explanation could link to day, but site pre-1960 octave language cannot change 1962 resolution. Intro paragraphs repeat between sources.

editorialDrafts.en: The Sunday after Easter is traditionally called in albis, recalling the white garments of those newly baptised at Easter. The Roman station at Saint Pancras, a young martyr, places their new life beside the witness of a Christian who remained faithful even at the cost of his life. The day's readings turn this image into a question for every baptised person: how is the faith received at baptism lived and defended?
editorialDrafts.fr: Le dimanche après Pâques est appelé in albis, en souvenir des vêtements blancs que portaient les nouveaux baptisés. La station romaine à Saint-Pancrace, jeune martyr, rapproche leur vie nouvelle du témoignage d'un chrétien demeuré fidèle jusqu'à la mort. Les lectures de ce dimanche donnent à cette image une portée durable : comment vivre et garder la foi reçue au baptême ?
editorialDrafts.verification: Check actual 1962 station and day's Proper Scripture passages against canonical resolver; verify history of vestment removal and wording, do not quote ICRSP translation.

editorialDrafts.en: The Mass of the Sacred Heart has not always used the same formulary. The devotion entered the universal Roman calendar in the nineteenth century, while a substantially revised Mass and Office were introduced under Pius XI in 1929. Earlier commentaries therefore sometimes explain prayers that are not those of the 1962 Missal. For the Mass actually celebrated, the approved Proper of the selected date remains the reference.
editorialDrafts.fr: La fête du Sacré-Cœur n'a pas toujours possédé le même formulaire. Son inscription au calendrier romain universel remonte au XIXᵉ siècle, tandis qu'une Messe et un Office largement remaniés furent introduits sous Pie XI en 1929. Les commentaires anciens expliquent donc parfois des prières différentes de celles du Missel de 1962. Pour la célébration effective, il faut se référer au propre approuvé du jour choisi.
editorialDrafts.verification: Verify 1856 and 1929 decrees, original site authorship and exact 1962 Proper name and calendar binding; submit human liturgical and translation review.
